title: Newspaper research progress, slave balls and Black musicians for white dances
summary: Kmen describes his newspaper research, slave balls, and Black musicians playing white dances but not vice versa.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: quite a few, all the books, descriptive books and memoirs through to the Civil War, but the most fruitful mine is in the newspapers, and this is very tedious work. You've got to go through them column by column, and I've gotten there into the close of the opera season of 1840, 1841, midway through 1841. Slaves even had, and I like to mention this while I think of it, but slaves, you see, even had balls that were acknowledged to be slave balls. This was, this was, dances, this was common here, and the very evening of the Civil War, one diary of a New Orleans family records that, how they were, everyone was excited because their slaves were dialing up to go to a slave ball, and you get some insight into the social relations because some of the people they were going with were free Negro, but married to the slaves, and all in all it was probably about four or five in this particular diary, and they were going to a ball which was celebrating the secession of Louisiana, which certainly shows that music comes first. Oh yeah. And dancing. And of course, one thing you're almost sure of, of course this is an inference, but everything I've read and studied makes me feel that Negro musicians would commonly play for white dances. I don't mean to say that Negroes played most of the white dances, but all white musicians played in the pre-Civil War days for dancing, but this didn't bother the Negro. Great men Negro musicians also played, and sometimes one dance hall might have Negro music on some nights and white music on other nights, but I feel quite certain that white musicians did not play for slave balls or pre-Negro balls, you see, so this in itself gave the

Negro wider feel. Well that condition exists until today, I mean really, the Negro bands play for both races, the white bands don't play for white. Yes. Well that brings up the point with me now, at what period did you say it became more fashionable for a man to go into business, a white band to go into business? Well there was some feeling about this all the way through,
